the design of a new class of antiviral agents, the 5‐thiophene‐ and 5‐oxothiophene‐1,2‐dithiazoles, which are inhibitors of the nucleocapsid (NC) protein of the feline immunodeﬁciency virus (FIV), an animal model for HIV.

the development of novel inhibitors of FIV and the identification of new classes of antiviral agents.

the 5‐oxodithiazoles are the most promising class of compounds for future development as antiviral agents.
the dithiazole derivatives are promising compounds with a novel mechanism of action that may serve as the basis for the development of new anti-HIV agents.
the dithiazole derivatives described in the manuscript are promising candidates to be developed into a new class of HIV and FIV inhibitors, with a novel mode of action.

The main takeaway from our work is that

5‐thio‐1,2‐dithiazoles are a promising new class of compounds that inhibit FIV and HIV by displacing zinc from the nucleocapsid protein, and that the thiazolyl‐thione group is the most important pharmacophore.

the 5‐oxa‐, 5−thia, and 5−imino‐1‐substituted‐2‐(4‐chloro‐phenyl)‐3‐(4‐methylphenyl)‐dithiazoles are a novel class of compounds that inhibit FIV in cells and may have potential as antiretroviral agents.

5‐thiophene‐ and 5‐oxazole‐substituted 1‐(2‐chloroethyl)‐1,2‐dithiole‐3‐thione derivatives are potent FIV inhibitors, and their activity is comparable to that of the lead compound, 2,2,4‐trimethylthiophene.
